goals: Find a maximum likelihood estimate in a simple case
Connect MLE to familiar loss functions
why: MLE is the principle behind logistic regression, Poisson regression, GMMs and most statistical models. Log-loss and MSE are likelihoods in disguise.
explain: A model with parameters can say how probable your observed data is. The **likelihood** is that probability, viewed as a function of the parameters.
**Maximum likelihood estimation** picks the parameters that make the observed data most probable: "turn the dials until the machine is most likely to produce what you actually saw."
In practice we maximise the **log-likelihood** (products become sums, which is easier and more numerically stable).
Hidden connections: with normal errors, maximising likelihood = minimising squared error (OLS). For yes/no outcomes it = minimising log-loss (logistic regression).

formula.plain: Choose the parameter value that gives the highest (log) probability to the observed data.

example.title: Conversion rate from 10 visitors
steps: Calculus confirms the maximum at p = 7/10 = 0.7
example.result: The MLE equals the sample proportion, matching intuition. The likelihood framework then extends to models with many parameters.

mistakes: Confusing likelihood with the probability of the parameter (that is Bayesian posterior territory).
Overfitting with tiny samples: MLE from 1 conversion out of 1 says p = 100%.
takeaways: Likelihood = how probable the data is under given parameters
OLS and log-loss are special cases

practice.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar
nll = lambda p: -(7 * np.log(p) + 3 * np.log(1 - p))     # negative log-likelihood
print(minimize_scalar(nll, bounds=(0.01, 0.99), method="bounded").x)   # ≈ 0.7

check.q: 3 defects in 100 items. MLE of the defect rate?
check.why: For binomial data the MLE is successes / trials.

check.q: With normally distributed errors, MLE for linear regression equals…
check.why: The normal log-likelihood is a negative sum of squared errors (scaled).
